title: Episode 170: Calvin Coolidge: The Homestead Inauguration and the Boston Police Strike (1919–1923)
description:
In the dead of night on August 3, 1923, deep in the rugged hills of Plymouth Notch, Vermont, an extraordinary scene played out inside a modest farmhouse without electricity or running water. By the amber flicker of a kerosene lamp, John Calvin Coolidge, a humble country notary public and justice of the peace, administered the oath of office of the President of the United States to his son, Calvin Coolidge, following the sudden death of Warren G. Harding. Four years earlier, as Governor of Massachusetts, Coolidge had been thrust onto the national stage when he broke the historic Boston Police Strike of 1919 with an immortal telegram: 'There is no right to strike against the public safety by anybody, anywhere, any time.' Discover the austere rise of America's thirtieth president.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the silent, principled world of America's thirtieth president, John Calvin Coolidge. In an age of roaring excess, political flamboyant showmanship, and sprawling federal power, Coolidge stood as an unyielding rock of Puritan discipline, dry humor, and quiet constitutional restraint. Here is George with the story of the Boston Police Strike, a midnight oath by kerosene lamp, and the ascent of Silent Cal.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE BOSTON POLICE STRIKE OF 1919
In September 1919, post-World War I America was convulsed by race riots, anarchist bombings, rampant inflation, and widespread industrial unrest. In Boston, tensions reached a boiling point when three-quarters of the city's fifteen hundred police officers voted to affiliate with the American Federation of Labor and walked off the job over meager wages and grueling eighty-hour workweeks. On the night of September 9, law and order in the historic cradle of liberty collapsed. Gangs of looters smashed plate-glass windows along Washington Street, dice games operated openly on street corners, and nightly robberies surged as terrified store owners guarded their wares with shotguns. When Boston Mayor Andrew Peters hesitated and allowed chaos to reign for forty-eight hours, Massachusetts Governor Calvin Coolidge intervened with decisive, quiet fury. Mobilizing the entire state militia, Coolidge took direct personal command of the capital city, restoring order with fixed bayonets and cavalry patrols. When union chief Samuel Gompers furiously protested that the strikers were being unfairly punished and demanded their reinstatement, Coolidge fired back an eight-word telegram that reverberated across the continent: 'There is no right to strike against the public safety by anybody, anywhere, any time.' In a single electric stroke, the unassuming Yankee governor became an overnight national hero, celebrated from coast to coast as the resolute champion of constitutional law and public order. The firm stance against public-sector walkouts established a precedent that would guide American labor jurisprudence for decades to come.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: PLYMOUTH NOTCH ROOTS AND THE PURITAN SOUL
Calvin Coolidge was born on the Fourth of July, 1872, in the tiny hamlet of Plymouth Notch, Vermont—a remote enclave of granite ledges, snowbound winters, and generational subsistence farming. His ancestry traced back to the earliest Puritan settlers of Massachusetts Bay in 1630, instilling in the young boy a deep reverence for thrift, unbending integrity, and the sanctity of the spoken word. His father, John Coolidge, was a prosperous farmer, storekeeper, and town magistrate whose word was sovereign law; his mother, Victoria, died when Calvin was only twelve years old, followed five years later by the tragic death of his beloved fifteen-year-old sister, Abigail. These devastating childhood bereavements cast an indelible mantle of solemn melancholy over the sensitive boy, driving him inward toward solitary contemplation. Graduating with high honors from Amherst College in Massachusetts, Coolidge chose to read law in Northampton rather than attend an elite law school. He married Grace Goodhue, a vibrant, warm-hearted teacher of deaf children whose radiant extroversion perfectly complemented his stoic, taciturn nature. Step by patient step, Coolidge climbed the political ladder: city councilman, city solicitor, state representative, mayor of Northampton, state senator, lieutenant governor, and ultimately governor. He never campaigned with extravagant promises, never slandered an opponent, and never spent a single dollar he could not account for, earning an unshakable reputation as a man whose silence spoke louder than other men's thunder. In an era when political oratory was frequently measured in bombastic hours, Coolidge's gift for absolute brevity was an astonishing superpower.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE 1920 CONVENTION AND THE VICE PRESIDENCY
When the Republican National Convention convened in Chicago in June 1920, the powerful party bosses—operating from the legendary smoke-filled suite at the Blackstone Hotel—had carefully engineered the presidential nomination of Ohio Senator Warren G. Harding. Intending to complete their slate with Wisconsin Senator Irvine Lenroot for the vice presidency, the bosses prepared to gavel the convention to a close. But as Lenroot's name was placed before the delegates, a weary, sweltering delegate from Oregon named Wallace McCamant leaped onto a chair. McCamant, who had been profoundly moved by Coolidge's handling of the Boston police strike and had read Coolidge's published speeches, shouted above the din: 'I nominate for the vice presidency Calvin Coolidge of Massachusetts!' A sudden, spontaneous roar swept through the Coliseum. The exhausted delegates, infuriated by the heavy-handed backroom dictation of the party oligarchy, staged an open rebellion. State after state switched its vote to Coolidge, sweeping the Massachusetts governor onto the national ticket with a staggering landslide. In November 1920, Harding and Coolidge crushed their Democratic opponents by a massive twenty-six-point popular vote margin. In Washington, Coolidge discovered the vice presidency to be a ceremonial wasteland. Harding generously invited him to attend cabinet meetings—a novel precedent in American governance—where Coolidge sat silently in a corner, absorbing every detail of federal administration while uttering hardly a syllable, observing the gathering storm clouds around Harding's reckless associates. His silent demeanor on the national stage earned him respect, as colleagues realized that every word he uttered was deliberate, measured, and true.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE MIDNIGHT TELEGRAM IN THE GREEN MOUNTAINS
In late July 1923, Calvin and Grace Coolidge retreated to Plymouth Notch for a summer vacation, assisting his aging father with the haying in the mountain meadows. On Thursday evening, August 2, the Vice President retired to bed early after an exhausting day of manual farm labor. The modest Coolidge homestead possessed neither electricity, telephone, nor indoor plumbing; news from the outside world traveled exclusively by horse and dirt road from the telegraph depot at Bridgewater. At two o'clock on Friday morning, August 3, the frantic clatter of a touring car broke the midnight silence of the mountain valley. Springfield reporter Leon Barrows and driver Erwin Geer screeched to a halt outside the farmhouse, pounding frantically on the wooden door. John Coolidge answered in his nightclothes, holding an oil lamp high above his head. Handed a Western Union telegram from San Francisco, the elder Coolidge climbed the creaking staircase to his son's bedroom and knocked gently. 'Calvin,' the old man whispered softly, 'President Harding is dead.' Without a word of alarm, Coolidge sat upright in bed. In that silent, heart-stopping instant, the enormous destiny of the United States fell squarely upon the shoulders of the quiet Vermont farm boy. In the quiet darkness of Plymouth Notch, the transfer of sovereign democratic authority occurred without a whisper of disorder or hesitation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE HOMESTEAD OATH BY KEROSENE LAMP
Dressing with deliberate, measured calm in a dark three-piece suit, Coolidge descended the narrow stairs to the parlor. His first act was to kneel beside Grace in prayer; his second was to draft a dignified statement of condolence to Florence Harding and a message of steady reassurance to the American people. But a critical constitutional question immediately arose: who had the legal authority to swear in the new chief executive? As telegrams arrived urging haste, John Coolidge remembered that he was a commissioned notary public and justice of the peace for the State of Vermont. After consulting by long-distance telephone from the local general store with Congressman Porter Dale and Attorney General Harry Daugherty, it was confirmed that a state magistrate possessed full legal power to administer the federal oath. At precisely two-forty-seven in the morning on August 3, 1923, a scene forever etched in American folklore unfolded in the modest parlor. By the soft yellow glow of a glass kerosene chimney lamp, with a hand-stitched quilt on the sofa and a wood-burning stove casting shadows against the wall, seventy-eight-year-old John Coolidge stood facing his fifty-one-year-old son across a small wooden table holding the family King James Bible. Raising his right hand, Calvin Coolidge repeated the timeless constitutional oath, sealing it with a quiet, heartfelt: 'So help me God.' Having become the thirtieth President of the United States, Calvin Coolidge walked back up the stairs, blew out the candle, and went calmly back to sleep. The humble surroundings of the homestead stood as a living symbol of the republican virtue upon which the United States had been founded.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: STEADYING THE SHIP OF STATE IN WASHINGTON
Coolidge arrived in Washington the following morning into a capital churning with vicious rumors, panic, and impending scandal. The sudden death of Harding had occurred just as the sickening stench of the Teapot Dome oil bribery, the Veterans' Bureau looting, and the Department of Justice corruption was beginning to permeate the public consciousness. Powerful politicians urged Coolidge to launch sweeping, theatrical purges to burnish his own political fortunes, while Harding loyalists begged him to suppress the congressional investigations. Coolidge did neither. Displaying an ice-cold, surgical impartiality, he announced that the law would take its course without fear or favor. When Attorney General Harry Daugherty refused to cooperate with Senate investigators, Coolidge demanded and secured his immediate resignation. To prosecute the oil magnates and cabinet conspirators, Coolidge took the groundbreaking step of appointing two distinguished special prosecutors—conservative Republican Owen Roberts and respected Democrat Atlee Pomerene—ensuring that the investigations were completely insulated from partisan politics. By refusing to panic, refusing to grandstand, and demonstrating absolute personal incorruptibility, Coolidge restored dignity and public confidence to the executive branch within six short months, transforming a national moral crisis into a triumph of constitutional stability. Coolidge demonstrated that quiet administrative resolve and absolute personal integrity are the most potent antidotes to public cynicism.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SOUL AND LEGACY OF SILENT CAL
Calvin Coolidge represented a philosophy of governance almost alien to the modern world: the supreme virtue of doing nothing unless strictly authorized by the Constitution. He famously remarked that four-fifths of all our troubles in this life would disappear if we would only sit down and keep still. Where other politicians measured success by the sheer volume of laws enacted, Coolidge took profound pride in the number of useless and meddlesome statutes he prevented from coming into being. He believed with religious fervor that the federal government should live within its means, pay off its war debts, lower the tax burden on ordinary citizens, and leave state governments and free individuals alone to cultivate their own fortunes. Under his steady hand, the United States stood upon the threshold of an unprecedented era of economic expansion, technological marvels, and cultural transformation. The silent farm boy from Plymouth Notch had assumed the helm of a wounded nation and, through the sheer gravity of character and quiet conviction, had made the American presidency once again a symbol of trust, honesty, and quiet strength. His presidency stands as an enduring monument to the philosophy that government exists to serve the citizen, not to command them.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Calvin Coolidge's midnight swearing-in by kerosene lamp remains one of the purest expressions of democratic continuity in American history. But having stabilized the republic after Harding's sudden death, Coolidge faced the daunting task of governing a rapidly modernizing nation during the frenetic Roaring Twenties. Next week, we examine the Coolidge presidency in full flower: the economic boom of the 1920s, 'Silent Cal's' legendary dry wit, the heartbreaking personal tragedy that shattered his private world, and his famous proclamation that 'the chief business of the American people is business.' Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
